title: Hello World Program
problem: Write a C program that "Hello, World!" to the console. This is the traditional first program used to verify a compiler setup works correctly.
requirements: Include stdio.h
Use printf to display the message
Return 0 from main
explanation: The program includes the standard I/O header, defines the main function as the entry point, and calls printf to output text to the console.
hint: Remember every C program needs a main() function as its entry point.

title: Add Two Numbers
problem: Write a program that reads two integers from the user and prints their sum.
requirements: Declare two integer variables
Read values using scanf
Compute and print the sum
explanation: Two integers are read using scanf, added together with the + operator, and the result is printed with printf.
hint: Use the & operator before variable names in scanf to pass their address.

title: Swap Two Numbers Using a Temporary Variable
problem: Write a program to swap the values of two variables using a third temporary variable.
requirements: Read two integers
Use a temp variable to swap them
Print values before and after swapping
outputExample:
Before: a=10, b=20
After: a=20, b=10
explanation: A temporary variable temporarily holds one value while the swap is performed, preventing data loss during reassignment.
output:
Before: a=10, b=20
After: a=20, b=10
hint: The temp variable acts as safe storage so no value is overwritten before it is used.

title: Swap Two Numbers Without a Temporary Variable
problem: Write a program that swaps two numbers using arithmetic operations instead of a third variable.
requirements: Read two integers
Swap using addition and subtraction (or XOR)
Print result
explanation: By adding both numbers into a and then subtracting appropriately, both values are exchanged without extra storage.
hint: Watch for integer overflow with very large numbers when using the addition method.

title: Simple Interest Calculator
problem: Write a program to calculate simple interest given principal, rate, and time using the formula SI = (P*R*T)/100.
requirements: Read principal, rate, and time as floats
Apply the simple interest formula
Print the result rounded to 2 decimals
explanation: The formula multiplies principal, rate, and time then divides by 100 to compute the interest earned.
hint: Use %.2f in printf to format floating point output to two decimal places.

title: Area and Circumference of a Circle
problem: Write a program that calculates the area and circumference of a circle given its radius.
requirements: Read radius as a float
Compute area using pi*r*r
Compute circumference using 2*pi*r
explanation: Using the mathematical constant pi (approximated as 3.14159), the program applies standard circle formulas.
hint: Declaring PI as const keeps the value fixed and communicates intent clearly.

title: Check Even or Odd
problem: Write a program that reads an integer and determines whether it is even or odd.
requirements: Read an integer
Use modulus operator to check divisibility by 2
Print appropriate message
explanation: The modulus operator % returns the remainder of division; a remainder of 0 when divided by 2 means the number is even.
hint: Any number n is even if (n % 2 == 0), regardless of sign.

title: Check Positive, Negative, or Zero
problem: Write a program that determines whether a number entered by the user is positive, negative, or zero.
requirements: Read an integer
Use if-else if-else to classify it
Print the classification
explanation: The program checks the number against zero using relational operators and prints the matching category.
hint: Order matters in else-if chains; check the most specific condition first if ranges overlap.

title: Largest of Two Numbers
problem: Write a program that reads two numbers and prints the larger one.
requirements: Read two integers
Compare them using an if-else statement
Print the larger value
explanation: A simple comparison determines which of the two variables holds the greater value.
hint: The ternary operator (a > b) ? a : b can shorten this comparison.

title: Largest of Three Numbers
problem: Write a program that reads three numbers and determines the largest among them.
requirements: Read three integers
Use nested if or logical operators to compare all three
Print the largest value
explanation: Nested conditionals compare each pair of numbers until the single largest value is identified.
hint: Using >= instead of > correctly handles cases where two numbers are equal and largest.

title: Simple Calculator Using Switch
problem: Write a calculator program that reads two numbers and an operator (+, -, *, /), then performs the corresponding operation using a switch statement.
requirements: Read two numbers and an operator character
Use switch-case to perform the operation
Handle division by zero and invalid operator cases
explanation: The switch statement branches based on the operator character, performing the matching arithmetic operation and handling edge cases like division by zero.
hint: Always check for division by zero before performing the division operation.

title: Print Multiplication Table
problem: Write a program that prints the multiplication table of a number entered by the user, from 1 to 10.
requirements: Read a number
Use a for loop from 1 to 10
Print each multiplication line
explanation: A for loop iterates from 1 to 10, multiplying the input number by the loop counter each time and printing the result.
hint: The loop counter i represents the multiplier and ranges from 1 through 10 inclusive.

title: Sum of Natural Numbers Using a Loop
problem: Write a program that calculates the sum of the first N natural numbers using a loop.
requirements: Read a positive integer N
Use a loop to accumulate the sum from 1 to N
Print the total sum
explanation: An accumulator variable starts at zero and is incremented by the loop counter on each iteration, producing the running total.
hint: The formula n*(n+1)/2 can verify your loop-based result.

title: Factorial Using a Loop
problem: Write a program that calculates the factorial of a number using an iterative loop.
requirements: Read a non-negative integer
Use a loop to multiply numbers from 1 to n
Print the factorial result
explanation: Starting with a product of 1, the loop multiplies it by each integer from 1 through n to compute n!.
hint: Use long long for the factorial variable since values grow very quickly.

title: Check Prime Number
problem: Write a program that checks whether a given number is a prime number.
requirements: Read an integer
Check divisibility from 2 up to sqrt(n)
Print whether it is prime or not
explanation: A number is prime if it has no divisors other than 1 and itself; the loop tests possible divisors up to its square root for efficiency.
hint: You only need to check divisors up to the square root of n, which greatly reduces the number of iterations.

title: Check Armstrong Number
problem: Write a program to check whether a given three-digit number is an Armstrong number (sum of cubes of its digits equals the number).
requirements: Read an integer
Extract each digit and cube it
Sum the cubes and compare to the original number
explanation: Each digit is extracted using modulus and division, cubed, and summed; if the sum equals the original number it is an Armstrong number.
hint: This example works for 3-digit Armstrong numbers; for other digit counts you'd raise each digit to the power of the digit count.

title: Reverse a Number
problem: Write a program that reverses the digits of an integer entered by the user.
requirements: Read an integer
Use a while loop to extract and rebuild digits in reverse
Print the reversed number
explanation: Each iteration extracts the last digit with modulus 10 and appends it to the reversed number, then removes the digit from the original with integer division.
hint: This same digit-reversal technique is the basis for palindrome-number checks.

title: Check Palindrome Number
problem: Write a program that checks whether a number reads the same forwards and backwards (a palindrome).
requirements: Read an integer
Reverse the number
Compare the reversed number to the original
explanation: The number is reversed using digit extraction, then compared to the original value to determine if it is a palindrome.
hint: Negative numbers need special handling since the minus sign complicates the reversal comparison.

title: Sum of Digits of a Number
problem: Write a program that calculates the sum of all digits of an integer.
requirements: Read an integer
Extract each digit using modulus and division
Accumulate and print the digit sum
explanation: The loop repeatedly extracts the last digit with % 10, adds it to a running total, then removes that digit using integer division by 10.
hint: This digit-sum pattern is reusable for digital-root and divisibility-by-9 checks.

title: Count Digits in a Number
problem: Write a program that counts how many digits are present in a given integer.
requirements: Read an integer
Use a loop to strip digits one at a time
Print the total digit count
explanation: Each loop iteration removes the last digit via integer division by 10 and increments a counter, until the number becomes zero.
hint: Remember to special-case 0, since the loop would otherwise count zero digits for it.

title: Print Fibonacci Series
problem: Write a program that prints the first N terms of the Fibonacci series using a loop.
requirements: Read the number of terms N
Generate terms using the sum of the previous two
Print all terms
explanation: Starting with 0 and 1, each subsequent Fibonacci term is the sum of the previous two terms, generated iteratively in a loop.
hint: Track only the last two terms in variables rather than storing the whole sequence to keep the solution memory-efficient.

title: Print Even Numbers in a Range
problem: Write a program that prints all even numbers between two numbers entered by the user.
requirements: Read start and end values
Loop through the range checking for evenness
Print each even number found
explanation: The loop iterates through every number in the range and uses the modulus operator to filter out only even numbers.
hint: You can also start the loop directly at the first even number and increment by 2 for efficiency.

title: Print Odd Numbers in a Range
problem: Write a program that prints all odd numbers between two numbers entered by the user.
requirements: Read start and end values
Loop through the range checking for oddness
Print each odd number found
explanation: The loop checks each number in the range and prints it only if the remainder when divided by 2 is not zero.
hint: This program mirrors the even-number version but flips the modulus condition.

title: Celsius to Fahrenheit Converter
problem: Write a program that converts a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit using the formula F = (C * 9/5) + 32.
requirements: Read temperature in Celsius
Apply the conversion formula
Print the Fahrenheit result
explanation: The formula scales the Celsius value by 9/5 and adds 32 to shift it into the Fahrenheit scale.
hint: Use 9.0/5.0 rather than 9/5 to avoid integer division truncating the ratio to 1.

title: Simple Grade Calculator
problem: Write a program that assigns a letter grade based on a student's numeric score using an else-if ladder.
requirements: Read a score between 0 and 100
Use else-if statements to determine the grade
Print the resulting letter grade
explanation: The else-if ladder checks the score against descending thresholds, assigning the first matching grade band.
hint: Check the highest grade band first since else-if stops at the first true condition.

title: Leap Year Checker
problem: Write a program to determine whether a given year is a leap year using the standard leap-year rules.
requirements: Read a year
Apply divisibility rules for 4, 100, and 400
Print whether it is a leap year
explanation: A year is a leap year if divisible by 4, except century years must also be divisible by 400 to qualify.
hint: Century years like 1900 are divisible by 4 but not leap years because they aren't divisible by 400.

title: ASCII Value of a Character
problem: Write a program that reads a character and displays its corresponding ASCII value.
requirements: Read a single character
Print its integer ASCII value using %d format specifier
explanation: Characters in C are stored internally as integers; using %d to print a char variable reveals its underlying ASCII code.
hint: Printing a char with %d implicitly converts it to its numeric ASCII representation.

title: Vowel or Consonant Checker
problem: Write a program that determines whether an entered alphabet letter is a vowel or a consonant.
requirements: Read a single character
Check against both uppercase and lowercase vowels
Print whether it's a vowel or consonant
explanation: The program compares the character against all vowel letters (upper and lower case) using logical OR conditions.
hint: Converting the character to lowercase first can simplify the comparison to just five checks.

title: Sum of Array Elements
problem: Write a program that reads N numbers into an array and calculates their sum.
requirements: Read array size N
Read N elements into an array
Loop through and sum all elements
explanation: Elements are stored in an array via a loop, then a second loop (or the same one) accumulates their total.
hint: C99 variable-length arrays let you size the array using a runtime value like n.

title: Find Maximum Element in an Array
problem: Write a program that finds the largest element in an array of N integers.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Track the maximum value seen while looping
Print the maximum element
explanation: The maximum is initialized to the first element, then updated whenever a larger element is found while scanning the array.
hint: Always initialize max to the first array element, not to zero, so negative-only arrays work correctly.

title: Find Minimum Element in an Array
problem: Write a program that finds the smallest element in an array of N integers.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Track the minimum value seen while looping
Print the minimum element
explanation: The minimum starts as the first element and is updated whenever a smaller element appears during the scan.
hint: This mirrors the maximum-finding pattern but flips the comparison direction.

title: Count Positive and Negative Numbers in an Array
problem: Write a program that counts how many positive and how many negative numbers exist in an array.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Use counters for positive and negative values
Print both counts
explanation: The loop checks each element's sign and increments the appropriate counter, ignoring zeros.
hint: Zero is neither positive nor negative, so it's naturally excluded by using else-if.

title: Reverse an Array
problem: Write a program that reverses the elements of an array in place.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Swap elements from both ends moving toward the center
Print the reversed array
explanation: Two indices start at opposite ends of the array and swap their values while moving toward each other until they meet.
hint: The loop only needs to run until i < j, since swapping past the midpoint would undo the reversal.

title: Linear Search in an Array
problem: Write a program that searches for a target value in an array using linear search and reports its index.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Read a target value to search for
Scan the array sequentially and report the index or 'not found'
explanation: Linear search checks each array element one by one from the start until the target is found or the array ends.
hint: Linear search works on unsorted data but runs in O(n) time; binary search is faster but requires sorted data.

title: Find String Length Without strlen
problem: Write a program that calculates the length of a string manually without using the strlen library function.
requirements: Read a string into a char array
Loop through characters until the null terminator is found
Print the count of characters
explanation: Strings in C are null-terminated; the loop counts characters until it encounters the '\0' terminator marking the end.
hint: Every C string ends with a hidden '\0' character; that's what the loop is detecting.

title: Copy a String Without strcpy
problem: Write a program that copies the contents of one string into another without using the strcpy library function.
requirements: Read a source string
Copy each character to a destination array manually
Terminate the destination string with a null character
explanation: Each character is copied one at a time in a loop, and a null terminator is manually appended at the end to complete the new string.
hint: Forgetting to add the terminating '\0' is a common bug that leaves the destination string malformed.

title: Concatenate Strings Without strcat
problem: Write a program that concatenates two strings without using the strcat library function.
requirements: Read two strings
Append the second string's characters to the end of the first manually
Print the concatenated result
explanation: The program finds the end of the first string, then copies each character of the second string starting from that position.
hint: Ensure the destination array str1 is large enough to hold both strings combined.

title: Check String Palindrome
problem: Write a program that checks whether a given string reads the same forwards and backwards.
requirements: Read a string
Compare characters from both ends moving inward
Print whether the string is a palindrome
explanation: Two pointers start at opposite ends of the string and compare characters, moving inward; a mismatch means it's not a palindrome.
hint: This same two-pointer technique works for checking array palindromes too.

title: Count Vowels in a String
problem: Write a program that counts the number of vowels present in a given string.
requirements: Read a string
Loop through each character checking if it's a vowel
Print the total vowel count
explanation: Each character is checked against both uppercase and lowercase vowels, incrementing a counter for every match found.
hint: The tolower() function from ctype.h can simplify vowel checks to just five comparisons.

title: Print Right Triangle Star Pattern
problem: Write a program that prints a right-angled triangle pattern made of stars, with a height entered by the user.
requirements: Read the number of rows
Use nested loops to print stars in increasing quantity per row
Print a newline after each row
explanation: The outer loop controls the row number and the inner loop prints that many stars, creating an increasing staircase pattern.
hint: The inner loop's upper bound equals the outer loop's current value, which is what produces the growing row width.

title: Print Pyramid Star Pattern
problem: Write a program that prints a centered pyramid pattern of stars using spaces and asterisks.
requirements: Read number of rows
Print leading spaces to center each row
Print increasing odd numbers of stars per row
explanation: Each row prints (rows - i) leading spaces followed by (2*i - 1) stars, which together produce a symmetric pyramid shape.
hint: Work out the space and star counts on paper for a small row count before coding the loop bounds.

title: Print Diamond Star Pattern
problem: Write a program that prints a diamond shape using stars by combining an upper pyramid and an inverted lower pyramid.
requirements: Read half-height of the diamond
Print the upper pyramid half
Print the inverted lower pyramid half
explanation: The top half prints a growing pyramid and the bottom half prints a shrinking inverted pyramid, together forming a diamond.
hint: Reuse the pyramid loop logic twice: once counting up, once counting down.

title: Print Pascal's Triangle
problem: Write a program that prints Pascal's Triangle up to a given number of rows, where each number is the sum of the two above it.
requirements: Read number of rows
Compute each entry using the binomial coefficient formula
Print the triangle with proper spacing
explanation: Each value in row i, column j equals C(i, j), calculated iteratively to avoid large factorial overflow.
hint: The iterative formula val = val*(i-j)/(j+1) computes binomial coefficients without needing large factorials.

title: GCD of Two Numbers Using Recursion
problem: Write a recursive function to find the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two numbers using the Euclidean algorithm.
requirements: Read two integers
Implement a recursive gcd function
Print the computed GCD
explanation: The Euclidean algorithm recursively replaces (a, b) with (b, a % b) until b becomes zero, at which point a is the GCD.
hint: The base case b == 0 is essential to stop the recursion; without it the function would recurse infinitely.

title: LCM of Two Numbers
problem: Write a program to find the least common multiple (LCM) of two numbers using their relationship to the GCD.
requirements: Read two integers
Compute their GCD
Calculate LCM using LCM = (a*b)/GCD
explanation: Since LCM(a,b) * GCD(a,b) = a*b, dividing the product of the two numbers by their GCD directly yields the LCM.
hint: Computing GCD first avoids overflow issues that can occur when finding LCM directly through brute force.

title: Power of a Number Using Recursion
problem: Write a recursive function that calculates the value of base raised to the power exponent.
requirements: Read a base and a non-negative exponent
Implement recursion where power(b,e) = b * power(b,e-1)
Print the result
explanation: The recursive case multiplies the base by the result of the power function called with the exponent decreased by one, until the exponent reaches zero.
hint: For very large exponents, a fast exponentiation (divide-and-conquer) approach reduces the recursion depth to O(log n).

title: Factorial Using Recursion
problem: Write a recursive function to compute the factorial of a non-negative integer.
requirements: Read an integer n
Implement recursion where factorial(n) = n * factorial(n-1)
Handle the base case factorial(0) = 1
explanation: The function calls itself with a decremented argument until it reaches the base case of 0, then multiplies results back up the call stack.
hint: Every recursive function needs a base case; without one, factorial would recurse until the stack overflows.

title: Fibonacci Series Using Recursion
problem: Write a recursive function that generates and prints the first N terms of the Fibonacci sequence.
requirements: Read the number of terms
Implement a recursive fibonacci function
Print each term using a loop that calls the recursive function
explanation: Each Fibonacci term is defined recursively as the sum of the two preceding terms, with base cases for the first two terms.
hint: This naive recursive version recalculates the same values repeatedly; memoization can make it much faster for large n.

title: Binary Search in a Sorted Array
problem: Write a program that searches for a target value in a sorted array using the binary search algorithm.
requirements: Read a sorted array of N elements
Read a target value
Use binary search to find its index, or report not found
explanation: Binary search repeatedly halves the search range by comparing the target to the middle element, discarding the half that cannot contain the target.
hint: Binary search requires the input array to be sorted; it runs in O(log n) time compared to linear search's O(n).

title: Bubble Sort
problem: Write a program that sorts an array of integers in ascending order using the bubble sort algorithm.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Repeatedly swap adjacent elements that are out of order
Print the sorted array
explanation: Bubble sort repeatedly passes through the array, swapping adjacent elements that are in the wrong order, until no swaps are needed.
hint: Bubble sort has O(n^2) time complexity, making it simple but inefficient for large datasets.

title: Selection Sort
problem: Write a program that sorts an array in ascending order using the selection sort algorithm.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Repeatedly find the minimum of the unsorted portion and swap it into place
Print the sorted array
explanation: Selection sort divides the array into sorted and unsorted parts, repeatedly selecting the minimum from the unsorted part and moving it to the end of the sorted part.
hint: Selection sort makes fewer swaps than bubble sort, which can be beneficial when writes are costly.

title: Insertion Sort
problem: Write a program that sorts an array in ascending order using the insertion sort algorithm.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Insert each element into its correct position within the sorted portion
Print the sorted array
explanation: Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time, shifting larger elements to the right to make room for the current element.
hint: Insertion sort performs well on nearly-sorted data, running close to O(n) in that best case.

title: Check Anagram Strings
problem: Write a program that checks whether two strings are anagrams of each other (contain the same characters with the same frequency).
requirements: Read two strings
Count the frequency of each character in both
Compare frequency counts to determine if they are anagrams
explanation: A 26-element frequency array tracks how many times each letter appears in the first string, then subtracts occurrences found in the second string; all zeros means an anagram.
hint: This solution assumes lowercase letters only; convert to lowercase first to handle mixed-case input.

title: Count Words in a Sentence
problem: Write a program that counts the number of words in a sentence entered by the user.
requirements: Read a full line of text including spaces
Count transitions from space to non-space characters
Print the total word count
explanation: The program scans the sentence and increments a counter each time it detects the start of a new word (a non-space character preceded by a space or the start of the line).
hint: fgets is used instead of scanf because it captures spaces, which are needed to detect word boundaries.

title: Remove Duplicate Characters from a String
problem: Write a program that removes duplicate characters from a string, keeping only the first occurrence of each character.
requirements: Read a string
Track which characters have already appeared using a boolean array
Build and print the string with duplicates removed
explanation: A seen[] array marks each character as encountered; characters are copied to the result only the first time they appear.
hint: Casting the character to unsigned char before indexing avoids negative index issues for extended ASCII values.

title: Find the Second Largest Element in an Array
problem: Write a program that finds the second largest distinct element in an array without sorting it.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Track the largest and second largest values in a single pass
Print the second largest value
explanation: Two variables track the largest and second largest seen so far; both are updated appropriately as each element is compared during a single traversal.
hint: This O(n) approach avoids the O(n log n) cost of sorting just to find the second largest value.

title: Matrix Addition
problem: Write a program that adds two matrices of the same dimensions and prints the resulting matrix.
requirements: Read dimensions and elements of two matrices
Add corresponding elements using nested loops
Print the resulting sum matrix
explanation: Nested loops iterate over every row and column index, adding the corresponding elements from both matrices into a result matrix.
hint: Matrix addition requires both matrices to have identical dimensions, unlike multiplication.

title: Matrix Multiplication
problem: Write a program that multiplies two compatible matrices and prints the resulting product matrix.
requirements: Read dimensions ensuring columns of first equal rows of second
Use three nested loops to compute the dot products
Print the resultant matrix
explanation: For each cell in the result, the program sums the products of corresponding row elements from the first matrix and column elements from the second matrix.
hint: Matrix multiplication is only defined when the number of columns in the first matrix equals the number of rows in the second.

title: Transpose of a Matrix
problem: Write a program that computes the transpose of a matrix by swapping its rows and columns.
requirements: Read a matrix of given dimensions
Create a transposed matrix where transpose[j][i] = original[i][j]
Print the transposed matrix
explanation: The transpose operation flips a matrix over its diagonal, turning rows into columns; element [i][j] becomes [j][i] in the new matrix.
hint: Notice the transposed matrix's dimensions are swapped (rows become columns) compared to the original.

title: Sum of Diagonal Elements of a Matrix
problem: Write a program that calculates the sum of both the primary and secondary diagonal elements of a square matrix.
requirements: Read a square matrix of size N
Sum elements where row index equals column index (primary)
Sum elements where row + col = N-1 (secondary)
outputExample:
Primary diagonal sum = 15
Secondary diagonal sum = 15
explanation: The primary diagonal consists of elements where the row index equals the column index; the secondary diagonal consists of elements where they sum to n-1.
output:
Primary diagonal sum = 15
Secondary diagonal sum = 15
hint: For odd-sized square matrices, the very center element belongs to both diagonals.

title: Structure to Store Student Details
problem: Write a program that defines a structure to store a student's name, roll number, and marks, then displays the details.
requirements: Define a struct Student with name, roll number, and marks
Read values into a struct variable
Print the stored student details
explanation: A structure groups related data of different types (string, int, float) under a single named type, making it easy to manage a student's record as one unit.
hint: Access structure members using the dot operator on a struct variable, e.g. s.name.

title: Array of Structures for Employee Records
problem: Write a program that stores multiple employee records using an array of structures, then displays all records.
requirements: Define a struct Employee with name, id, and salary
Read details for N employees into an array of structs
Print all employee records
outputExample:
ID: 1, Name: Alice, Salary: 50000.00
ID: 2, Name: Bob, Salary: 55000.00
explanation: An array of structures allows storing multiple records of the same composite type, each accessed by index like emp[i].name.
output:
ID: 1, Name: Alice, Salary: 50000.00
ID: 2, Name: Bob, Salary: 55000.00
hint: An array of structs is ideal when you need to manage many records that share the same set of fields.

title: Swap Two Numbers Using Pointers
problem: Write a program that swaps two numbers using pointers and a function, demonstrating pass-by-reference.
requirements: Write a swap function that accepts two int pointers
Dereference the pointers to exchange values
Call the function passing addresses of two variables
outputExample:
Before: a=5, b=10
After: a=10, b=5
explanation: Passing pointers to the swap function lets it modify the original variables directly through dereferencing, rather than working on local copies.
output:
Before: a=5, b=10
After: a=10, b=5
hint: In C, pass-by-reference is achieved by passing a pointer (address) rather than the value itself.

title: Pointer Arithmetic Example
problem: Write a program that demonstrates pointer arithmetic by traversing an array using a pointer instead of index notation.
requirements: Declare an array and a pointer to its first element
Use pointer increment to move through the array
Print each element via pointer dereferencing
explanation: Incrementing a pointer moves it forward by the size of the type it points to, allowing traversal of the array without using index brackets.
hint: The array name itself decays to a pointer to its first element, so arr and &arr[0] are equivalent.

title: Function Pointers Example
problem: Write a program that demonstrates function pointers by storing addresses of arithmetic functions and calling them dynamically.
requirements: Define add and subtract functions
Declare a function pointer and assign it to each function
Call the functions through the pointer
explanation: A function pointer stores the address of a function, allowing it to be called indirectly, which is useful for callbacks and dynamic dispatch.
hint: The declaration int (*operation)(int, int) reads as 'operation is a pointer to a function taking two ints and returning an int'.

title: Recursive Sum of Array Elements
problem: Write a recursive function that calculates the sum of all elements in an array.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Implement recursion that sums arr[0] plus the recursive sum of the rest
Print the total sum
explanation: The recursive function adds the first element to the result of calling itself on the remaining sub-array, with an empty array (index == size) as the base case.
hint: Each recursive call reduces the problem size by one element until reaching the base case of an empty array.

title: Check Perfect Number
problem: Write a program to check whether a given number is a perfect number (equal to the sum of its proper divisors).
requirements: Read an integer
Find all proper divisors and sum them
Compare the sum to the original number
explanation: A number is perfect if the sum of its divisors (excluding itself) equals the number; the loop checks every number from 1 up to n-1 for divisibility.
hint: Checking divisors only up to sqrt(n) and adding both the divisor and its pair can make this more efficient.

title: Check Strong Number
problem: Write a program to check whether a given number is a strong number (the sum of the factorials of its digits equals the number).
requirements: Read an integer
Compute the factorial of each digit and sum them
Compare the sum to the original number
explanation: Each digit's factorial is computed and summed; strong numbers like 145 satisfy 1! + 4! + 5! = 1 + 24 + 120 = 145.
hint: 145 and 40585 are well-known strong numbers you can use to test the program.

title: Print All Prime Numbers in a Range Using Sieve of Eratosthenes
problem: Write a program that prints all prime numbers up to N using the Sieve of Eratosthenes algorithm.
requirements: Read an upper limit N
Create a boolean array marking non-primes by elimination
Print all numbers that remain marked as prime
explanation: The sieve marks multiples of each prime starting from 2 as composite; whatever numbers remain unmarked at the end are prime.
hint: The sieve runs in O(n log log n) time, making it much faster than checking each number individually for primality.

title: Convert Decimal to Binary
problem: Write a program that converts a decimal (base 10) number to its binary (base 2) representation.
requirements: Read a decimal integer
Repeatedly divide by 2 and store remainders
Print the remainders in reverse order as the binary result
explanation: Dividing the number by 2 repeatedly and collecting the remainders (0 or 1) produces the binary digits in reverse order, which are then printed backwards.
hint: Store remainders in an array first since they're generated in reverse order relative to how binary numbers are written.

title: Convert Binary to Decimal
problem: Write a program that converts a binary number (entered as a sequence of digits) to its decimal equivalent.
requirements: Read a binary number as an integer or string
Multiply each digit by the appropriate power of 2
Sum the results to get the decimal value
explanation: Starting from the rightmost binary digit, each digit is multiplied by an increasing power of 2 and the products are summed to get the decimal value.
hint: Reading the binary number as an integer works for simple cases but a string-based approach is safer for very long binary sequences.

title: Convert Decimal to Hexadecimal
problem: Write a program that converts a decimal number to its hexadecimal (base 16) representation.
requirements: Read a decimal integer
Repeatedly divide by 16, mapping remainders 10-15 to A-F
Print the hex digits in the correct order
explanation: Dividing repeatedly by 16 produces remainders 0-15; remainders above 9 are mapped to letters A through F to form valid hexadecimal digits.
hint: You could also use printf("%X", n) directly, but implementing it manually reinforces the underlying conversion logic.

title: String Tokenization Using strtok
problem: Write a program that splits a sentence into individual words (tokens) using the strtok library function.
requirements: Read a line of text
Use strtok with space as the delimiter to extract tokens
Print each token on a separate line
explanation: strtok scans the string for delimiter characters, replacing them with null terminators and returning a pointer to each token in sequence across repeated calls.
hint: After the first call, pass NULL as the first argument to strtok to continue tokenizing the same string.

title: Command Line Arguments Example
problem: Write a program that reads and displays command-line arguments passed to it when executed.
requirements: Use argc and argv parameters in main
Print the count of arguments
Loop through and print each argument
outputExample:
Number of arguments: 3
Argument 0: ./program
Argument 1: hello
Argument 2: world
explanation: argc holds the count of command-line arguments and argv is an array of strings containing them, with argv[0] always being the program name itself.
output:
Number of arguments: 3
Argument 0: ./program
Argument 1: hello
Argument 2: world
hint: argv[0] is conventionally the executable's name, so actual user-supplied arguments start at argv[1].

title: Bitwise Operators Demonstration
problem: Write a program that demonstrates the use of bitwise AND, OR, XOR, NOT, left shift, and right shift operators on two integers.
requirements: Read two integers
Apply each bitwise operator
Print the results of all operations
outputExample:
AND = 8
OR = 14
XOR = 6
NOT a = -13
Left Shift = 24
Right Shift = 3
explanation: Bitwise operators manipulate the individual binary bits of integers directly: AND keeps common bits, OR combines bits, XOR keeps differing bits, and shifts move bits left or right.
output:
AND = 8
OR = 14
XOR = 6
NOT a = -13
Left Shift = 24
Right Shift = 3
hint: Left shift by 1 doubles a number and right shift by 1 halves it (for non-negative integers), similar to multiplying or dividing by 2.

title: Dynamic Array Using malloc
problem: Write a program that dynamically allocates an array at runtime using malloc, fills it with user input, and frees the memory afterward.
requirements: Read the desired array size
Allocate memory using malloc
Fill, print, and then free the array
explanation: malloc allocates a block of heap memory large enough for n integers; this memory persists until explicitly released with free, unlike stack-based arrays.
hint: Always check malloc's return value for NULL and call free() once you're done to avoid memory leaks.

title: Dynamic 2D Array Using malloc
problem: Write a program that dynamically allocates a 2D array (matrix) at runtime using malloc and demonstrates reading and printing it.
requirements: Read rows and columns
Allocate an array of row pointers, each pointing to a dynamically allocated row
Fill, print, and then free all allocated memory
explanation: A dynamic 2D array is built as an array of pointers, where each pointer is separately allocated to point to its own dynamically sized row of columns.
hint: Free each row individually before freeing the outer pointer array to prevent leaking the row memory.

title: Resizable Array Using realloc
problem: Write a program that starts with a small dynamically allocated array and grows it using realloc as more elements are added.
requirements: Allocate an initial small array with malloc
Use realloc to expand its capacity when needed
Fill and print the resized array
explanation: realloc resizes a previously allocated memory block, preserving existing contents while extending (or shrinking) the available space as needed.
hint: Doubling the capacity each time an array fills up gives amortized O(1) insertion, a common strategy behind dynamic array implementations.

title: Singly Linked List - Insert and Display
problem: Write a program that implements a singly linked list, allowing nodes to be inserted at the end and the full list to be displayed.
requirements: Define a node structure with data and a next pointer
Implement an insert function that appends nodes to the end
Implement a display function to print all nodes
explanation: Each node dynamically allocated holds a data value and a pointer to the next node; insertion traverses to the last node and links the new node after it.
hint: The head pointer must be updated when inserting into an empty list, which is why insert() returns the (possibly new) head.

title: Linked List - Delete a Node
problem: Write a program that deletes a node with a specific value from a singly linked list.
requirements: Build a linked list from user input
Implement a delete function that removes the first node matching a target value
Display the list before and after deletion
explanation: Deletion requires tracking the previous node so its next pointer can be rerouted around the node being removed, then freeing that node's memory.
hint: Special-case deleting the head node separately, since it has no previous node to update.

title: Reverse a Linked List
problem: Write a program that reverses a singly linked list in place by reversing the direction of each node's next pointer.
requirements: Build a linked list from user input
Iterate through the list reversing next pointers
Display the list before and after reversal
explanation: Three pointers (previous, current, next) walk through the list, redirecting each node's next pointer to point backward instead of forward.
hint: This iterative reversal runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, without needing recursion or an auxiliary list.

title: Stack Implementation Using an Array
problem: Write a program that implements a stack (LIFO data structure) using a fixed-size array, supporting push, pop, and peek operations.
requirements: Define a stack with a fixed-size array and a top index
Implement push, pop, and peek functions with overflow/underflow checks
Demonstrate the operations with sample data
explanation: The stack's top variable tracks the index of the most recently added element; push increments it before inserting, and pop returns the element then decrements it.
hint: Always check for overflow before pushing and underflow before popping to avoid accessing invalid array indices.

title: Stack Implementation Using a Linked List
problem: Write a program that implements a stack using a singly linked list, allowing dynamic growth without a fixed size limit.
requirements: Define a node structure for stack elements
Implement push and pop operations that insert/remove from the head
Demonstrate pushing and popping several values
explanation: Using the head of a linked list as the stack's top avoids the fixed capacity limitation of an array-based stack; push adds a new head, pop removes and frees it.
hint: A linked-list-based stack has no fixed maximum size, limited only by available heap memory.

title: Queue Implementation Using an Array
problem: Write a program that implements a queue (FIFO data structure) using an array, supporting enqueue and dequeue operations.
requirements: Define a queue with front and rear indices
Implement enqueue and dequeue with overflow/underflow checks
Demonstrate the operations with sample data
explanation: The rear index tracks where the next element is inserted and the front index tracks where the next element is removed, implementing first-in-first-out ordering.
hint: This simple array-based queue doesn't reuse freed space at the front; a circular queue solves that limitation.

title: Queue Implementation Using a Linked List
problem: Write a program that implements a queue using a singly linked list with separate front and rear pointers.
requirements: Define a node structure and maintain front and rear pointers
Implement enqueue (insert at rear) and dequeue (remove from front)
Demonstrate the operations with sample data
explanation: The rear pointer allows O(1) insertion at the end of the list, while the front pointer allows O(1) removal from the beginning, giving efficient FIFO behavior.
hint: Remember to reset rear to NULL when the last element is dequeued, or rear will point to freed memory.

title: Circular Queue Implementation
problem: Write a program that implements a circular queue using an array, where the rear wraps around to reuse space freed by dequeued elements.
requirements: Define a fixed-size array with front, rear, and count tracking
Implement enqueue and dequeue using modulus for wrap-around
Demonstrate filling, dequeuing, and reusing space
explanation: The rear index advances using (rear + 1) % size, allowing it to wrap back to index 0 once it reaches the end, reusing slots freed by dequeue operations.
hint: The condition (rear + 1) % SIZE == front detects a full queue, distinguishing it from the empty state where front == -1.

title: Binary Tree - Insert and Inorder Traversal
problem: Write a program that builds a binary search tree by inserting values and then prints its elements using inorder traversal.
requirements: Define a tree node structure with left and right child pointers
Implement a recursive insert function maintaining BST order
Implement recursive inorder traversal to print sorted output
explanation: Insertion recursively places smaller values in the left subtree and larger values in the right subtree; inorder traversal (left, root, right) visits nodes in sorted order.
hint: Inorder traversal of a binary search tree always produces elements in ascending sorted order.

title: Binary Search Tree - Search Operation
problem: Write a program that builds a binary search tree and implements a recursive search function to check if a value exists in it.
requirements: Build a BST from user input using recursive insertion
Implement a recursive search function
Report whether a target value was found
explanation: The search function compares the target to the current node, recursing left if smaller or right if larger, exploiting the BST's ordering property to skip half the tree at each step.
hint: BST search runs in O(log n) on average for a balanced tree, but degrades to O(n) for a skewed (unbalanced) tree.

title: Quick Sort Implementation
problem: Write a program that sorts an array in ascending order using the quicksort algorithm with the Lomuto partition scheme.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Implement a partition function using a pivot element
Recursively sort the sub-arrays on either side of the pivot
explanation: Quicksort selects a pivot, partitions the array so smaller elements come before it and larger elements after, then recursively sorts each partition.
hint: Quicksort has an average time complexity of O(n log n) but can degrade to O(n^2) on already-sorted input with a poor pivot choice.

title: Merge Sort Implementation
problem: Write a program that sorts an array in ascending order using the merge sort algorithm.
requirements: Read N elements into an array
Recursively divide the array into halves
Merge the sorted halves back together
explanation: Merge sort recursively splits the array into halves until single elements remain, then merges sorted halves together by repeatedly picking the smaller front element.
hint: Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) time in all cases, unlike quicksort's worst-case O(n^2), but requires additional memory for the temporary arrays.

title: File Handling - Write to a File
problem: Write a program that takes text input from the user and writes it to a file on disk.
requirements: Open a file in write mode using fopen
Write user-entered text to the file using fprintf
Close the file properly
explanation: fopen with mode "w" creates a new file (or overwrites an existing one) for writing; fprintf writes formatted text to it, and fclose flushes and releases the file handle.
hint: Always check that fopen did not return NULL before attempting to write, since the file might fail to open due to permissions or disk issues.

title: File Handling - Read from a File
problem: Write a program that reads and displays the contents of a text file line by line.
requirements: Open an existing file in read mode
Use fgets in a loop to read each line
Print each line and close the file
explanation: fopen with mode "r" opens an existing file for reading; fgets reads one line at a time into a buffer until it returns NULL at end-of-file.
hint: Reading mode "r" requires the file to already exist; attempting to open a missing file returns NULL from fopen.

title: File Handling - Append to a File
problem: Write a program that appends new text to the end of an existing file without overwriting its current contents.
requirements: Open a file in append mode using fopen with 'a'
Write new text to the end of the file
Close the file and confirm the operation
explanation: Append mode "a" positions the file pointer at the end of the existing file, so any writes are added after the current content rather than replacing it.
hint: If the file doesn't exist yet, append mode "a" will create it, behaving like write mode in that case.

title: Copy File Contents to Another File
problem: Write a program that copies the entire contents of one file into a new destination file.
requirements: Open a source file in read mode and a destination file in write mode
Copy content character by character using fgetc and fputc
Close both files and confirm success
explanation: The program reads one character at a time from the source file with fgetc and writes it immediately to the destination file with fputc, continuing until EOF is reached.
hint: For large files, reading in larger chunks with fread/fwrite is more efficient than one character at a time.

title: Structure with Pointers - Dynamic Student Records
problem: Write a program that dynamically allocates an array of student structures using malloc and a pointer to the structure type.
requirements: Define a Student structure with name and marks
Dynamically allocate an array of N students using malloc
Fill and display records using pointer-based struct access, then free memory
explanation: Using struct Student *students = malloc(n * sizeof(struct Student)) creates a dynamically-sized array of structs, accessed with the arrow operator (students[i].field or (students+i)->field).
hint: Both students[i].field and (students+i)->field are equivalent ways to access array-of-struct elements through a pointer.

title: Union Demonstration
problem: Write a program that demonstrates how a union shares the same memory location among its members, unlike a structure.
requirements: Define a union with an int, float, and char member
Assign and print each member, observing how memory is shared
Print the size of the union
outputExample:
Union size: 4 bytes
After assigning int: 10
After assigning float: 15.750000
explanation: All members of a union occupy the same memory address, so writing to one member overwrites the value of any other member; the union's size equals its largest member.
output:
Union size: 4 bytes
After assigning int: 10
After assigning float: 15.750000
hint: Unlike structures where each member gets its own memory, a union's members overlap, making it memory-efficient when only one value is needed at a time.

title: Enum Demonstration
problem: Write a program that demonstrates how enumerations create a set of named integer constants, using days of the week as an example.
requirements: Define an enum for days of the week
Assign an enum value to a variable
Use a switch statement to print the day name
explanation: An enum assigns sequential integer values (starting at 0 by default) to a list of named identifiers, making code more readable than using raw magic numbers.
hint: By default enum values start at 0 and increment by 1, but you can explicitly assign custom starting values or specific numbers to each constant.

title: Variable Length Arguments Using stdarg.h
problem: Write a program that defines a function accepting a variable number of integer arguments and calculates their sum using the stdarg.h library.
requirements: Use va_list, va_start, va_arg, and va_end from stdarg.h
Write a function that sums an arbitrary number of integers
Call the function with different numbers of arguments
outputExample:
Sum of 3 numbers = 6
Sum of 5 numbers = 15
explanation: Variadic functions use va_list to iterate over an unspecified number of arguments; va_start initializes the list, va_arg retrieves each value, and va_end cleans up.
output:
Sum of 3 numbers = 6
Sum of 5 numbers = 15
hint: The first parameter (count here) is typically used to tell the function how many variadic arguments follow, since C has no built-in way to know this automatically.

title: Simple Student Management System (Mini Project)
problem: Build a menu-driven console application that allows adding, displaying, and searching student records stored in memory using structures and arrays.
requirements: Define a Student structure with name, roll number, and marks
Implement a menu loop with options to add, display, and search students
Use a fixed-size array of structures to store up to 50 students
outputExample:
Student added successfully.
Name: John, Roll: 101, Marks: 88.50
explanation: The program combines structures for record storage, arrays for the record list, and a switch-based menu loop to let the user choose operations interactively until they exit.
output:
Student added successfully.
Name: John, Roll: 101, Marks: 88.50
hint: Breaking each menu option into its own function keeps main() readable and makes the program easier to extend with new features.

title: Simple Bank Account Management System (Mini Project)
problem: Build a menu-driven console application that simulates basic bank operations: creating an account, depositing, withdrawing, and checking balance.
requirements: Define an Account structure with holder name and balance
Implement deposit and withdraw functions with balance validation
Provide a menu loop for the user to perform operations until exiting
outputExample:
Account created for Alice with balance 1000.00
Deposited 500.00. New balance: 1500.00
Withdrew 200.00. New balance: 1300.00
Current balance: 1300.00
explanation: The program stores account data in a structure and provides functions for each banking operation, with withdraw specifically validating that sufficient funds exist before deducting.
output:
Account created for Alice with balance 1000.00
Deposited 500.00. New balance: 1500.00
Withdrew 200.00. New balance: 1300.00
Current balance: 1300.00
hint: Validating the withdrawal amount against the current balance before subtracting prevents the account from going negative.
